stem: Let \(p(x) = x^3 - 3x + k\), where \(k \in \mathbb{R}\). You may use \(p'(x) = 3x^2 - 3\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that if \((x - \alpha)^2\) is a factor of a polynomial \(q(x)\), then \(q(\alpha) = 0\) and \(q'(\alpha) = 0\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the two values of \(k\) for which \(p(x) = 0\) has a repeated root, and for each one write \(p(x)\) as a product of linear factors.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of distinct real roots of \(p(x) = 0\) when \(|k| < 2\), when \(|k| = 2\) and when \(|k| > 2\). Justify your answer.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Let \(k = 1\), and let the roots of \(p(x) = 0\) be \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\). Find a cubic equation with integer coefficients whose roots are \(\alpha^2\), \(\beta^2\) and \(\gamma^2\).

idea: A repeated root is a root of both \(p\) and \(p'\). The roots of \(p(x) = 0\) are where the line \(y = -k\) meets \(y = x^3 - 3x\), whose turning values are \(\pm 2\). For new roots, find their sum, their pairwise sum and their product from the old ones.

solution.label: a
steps: Write \(q(x) = (x - \alpha)^2 r(x)\). Then \(q(\alpha) = 0\), and by the product rule \(q'(x) = 2(x - \alpha)r(x) + (x - \alpha)^2 r'(x)\), so \(q'(\alpha) = 0\).

solution.label: c
steps: \(p(x) = 0\) means \(x^3 - 3x = -k\). The graph of \(y = x^3 - 3x\) has a local maximum 2 at \(x = -1\) and a local minimum \(-2\) at \(x = 1\).
The horizontal line \(y = -k\) meets it three times if \(-2 < -k < 2\), twice (one point a tangent) if \(-k = \pm 2\), and once otherwise.

stem: The equation \(x^2 - px + q = 0\) has roots \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Let \(S_n = \alpha^n + \beta^n\), for \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(S_{n+2} = pS_{n+1} - qS_n\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Now let \(p = 1\) and \(q = -1\). Find \(S_0, S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_6\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: For these values of \(p\) and \(q\), prove that \(S_n\) is an integer for every \(n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\)

parts.label: d
parts.text: The roots are \(\alpha = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}\) and \(\beta = \dfrac{1 - \sqrt{5}}{2}\). Given that \(S_{10} = 123\), and using \(|\beta| < \dfrac{2}{3}\), show that \(122.98 < \alpha^{10} < 123\).

idea: Each root satisfies its own equation: \(\alpha^2 = p\alpha - q\). Multiply by \(\alpha^n\), do the same for \(\beta\), and add. Then \(\alpha^{10} = 123 - \beta^{10}\), and \(\beta^{10}\) is a small positive number.

solution.label: a
steps: \(\alpha^2 = p\alpha - q\), so \(\alpha^{n+2} = p\alpha^{n+1} - q\alpha^n\). Likewise \(\beta^{n+2} = p\beta^{n+1} - q\beta^n\).

solution.label: c
steps: \(S_0 = 2\) and \(S_1 = 1\) are integers. If \(S_k\) and \(S_{k+1}\) are integers, then \(S_{k+2} = S_{k+1} + S_k\) is an integer.
So by induction (on consecutive pairs), \(S_n\) is an integer for every \(n\).

stem: The concentration of a medicine in a patient’s blood, \(t\) hours after a dose, is modelled by \(C(t) = \dfrac{20t}{t^2 + 4}\) mg per litre, for \(t \ge 0\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down \(C(0)\), and describe what happens to \(C(t)\) as \(t\) increases without limit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: By writing \(C(t) = k\) as a quadratic in \(t\), show that \(C(t) \le 5\) for all \(t \ge 0\), and find when the maximum concentration occurs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The medicine is effective when its concentration is above 4 mg per litre. Find the length of time for which it is effective.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A second, identical dose is taken 3 hours after the first, and the concentrations add, so that for \(t \ge 3\) the total is \(C(t) + C(t - 3)\). Find the greatest total concentration and the time at which it occurs.

parts.label: e
parts.text: After the second dose, find the time at which the total concentration falls below 1 mg per litre for the last time.

idea: A value \(k\) is reached exactly when \(kt^2 - 20t + 4k = 0\) has a real root, so the discriminant gives the greatest possible \(k\). With two doses the total is \(C(t) + C(t - 3)\) for \(t \ge 3\), which needs a GDC.

solution.label: a
steps: \(C(0) = 0\). For large \(t\) the denominator grows faster than the numerator, so \(C(t) \to 0\).

solution.label: b
steps: \(\dfrac{20t}{t^2 + 4} = k\) gives \(kt^2 - 20t + 4k = 0\). For \(k \ne 0\) a real \(t\) needs \(400 - 16k^2 \ge 0\), so \(k \le 5\) (concentrations are not negative).
solution.answer: Maximum 5 mg per litre, at \(t = 2\) hours

solution.label: d
steps: For \(t \ge 3\) the total is \(T(t) = \dfrac{20t}{t^2 + 4} + \dfrac{20(t - 3)}{(t - 3)^2 + 4}\). With a GDC, the maximum is \(8.538\ldots\) at \(t = 4.665\ldots\)

solution.label: e
steps: \(T(t)\) decreases after its maximum. Solve \(T(t) = 1\) for \(t > 4.67\) with a GDC: \(t = 41.45\ldots\)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(f\) is an even function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down the equations of the asymptotes of the graph of \(f\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the points where the graph of \(f\) meets the axes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the range of \(f\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Solve the inequality \(f(x) \ge 2\).

idea: Make \(x^2\) the subject of \(f(x) = y\): a value \(y\) is in the range exactly when the expression for \(x^2\) is non-negative (and \(x \ne \pm 2\)). For the inequality, collect everything into one fraction and use signs.

solution.label: b
steps: Vertical: \(x^2 - 4 = 0\), \(x = \pm 2\) (the numerator is 3 there). Horizontal: the leading coefficients of top and bottom are both 1, so \(y = 1\).

solution.label: d
steps: \(y\left(x^2 - 4\right) = x^2 - 1\) gives \(x^2(y - 1) = 4y - 1\), so for \(y \ne 1\), \(x^2 = \dfrac{4y - 1}{y - 1}\). (\(y = 1\) would need \(3 = 0\): impossible.)
Need \(\dfrac{4y - 1}{y - 1} \ge 0\): \(y \le \frac{1}{4}\) or \(y > 1\). (This value of \(x^2\) is never 4, since that would need \(4y - 4 = 4y - 1\).)

solution.label: e
steps: Top \(\ge 0\) when \(x^2 \le 7\); bottom \(> 0\) when \(x^2 > 4\). Both negative: \(x^2 > 7\) and \(x^2 < 4\), impossible. So \(4 < x^2 \le 7\).

stem: A function \(f\) is self-inverse if \((f \circ f)(x) = x\) for every \(x\) in its domain. Consider \(f(x) = \dfrac{ax + b}{cx + d}\), where \(a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{R}\), \(c \ne 0\) and \(ad - bc \ne 0\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(g(x) = \dfrac{2x + 3}{x - 2}\), for \(x \ne 2\), is self-inverse.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that \((f \circ f)(x) = \dfrac{\left(a^2 + bc\right)x + b(a + d)}{c(a + d)x + bc + d^2}\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence show that \(f\) is self-inverse if \(a + d = 0\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the value of \(k\) for which \(h(x) = \dfrac{kx + 1}{x + 3}\) is self-inverse, and state the domain and range of \(h\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: For this value of \(k\), find the exact coordinates of the points where the graph of \(h\) meets the line \(y = x\).

idea: Compose by substituting the fraction into itself and clearing the inner denominators. A self-inverse function is its own inverse, so its domain and range are the same set, and its graph is symmetric in \(y = x\).

solution.label: a
steps: \(g(g(x)) = \dfrac{2\cdot\frac{2x + 3}{x - 2} + 3}{\frac{2x + 3}{x - 2} - 2}\). Multiply top and bottom by \(x - 2\): \(\dfrac{4x + 6 + 3x - 6}{2x + 3 - 2x + 4} = \dfrac{7x}{7} = x\).

solution.label: b
steps: \(f(f(x)) = \dfrac{a\frac{ax + b}{cx + d} + b}{c\frac{ax + b}{cx + d} + d}\). Multiply top and bottom by \(cx + d\):
Top: \(a(ax + b) + b(cx + d) = \left(a^2 + bc\right)x + b(a + d)\). Bottom: \(c(ax + b) + d(cx + d) = c(a + d)x + bc + d^2\).

solution.label: c
steps: If \(d = -a\): the top is \(\left(a^2 + bc\right)x\) and the bottom is \(bc + a^2\). Since \(ad - bc = -\left(a^2 + bc\right) \ne 0\), this is \(x\).

solution.label: d
steps: Domain \(x \ne -3\). A self-inverse function has range equal to its domain: \(h(x) = -3 + \frac{10}{x + 3}\) never equals \(-3\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sketch the graph of \(y = g(x)\), showing its vertex and the points where it meets the axes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sketch the graph of \(y = g(|x|)\), showing its local maximum and minimum points and the points where it meets the axes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sketch the graph of \(y = \left|g(|x|)\right|\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the number of solutions of the equation \(\left|g(|x|)\right| = 3\).

parts.label: e
parts.text: Find the set of values of \(k\) for which the equation \(\left|g(|x|)\right| = k\) has exactly six solutions.

idea: \(g(|x|)\) keeps the right half of the parabola and mirrors it in the \(y\)-axis; the outer modulus then reflects the negative parts up. Count solutions by sliding a horizontal line across the final graph, paying attention to the heights of its turning points (3 at \(x = 0\), 4 at \(x = \pm 1\)).

solution.label: b
steps: For \(x \ge 0\) use \(g(x)\); reflect in the \(y\)-axis. Minimum points \((\pm 1, -4)\), a corner at \((0, -3)\), \(x\)-intercepts \((\pm 3, 0)\).
solution.answer: W shape: minima \((\pm 1, -4)\), local maximum (corner) \((0, -3)\), zeros at \(x = \pm 3\)

solution.label: c
steps: Reflect the part between \(x = -3\) and \(x = 3\) up: maxima \((\pm 1, 4)\), a corner at \((0, 3)\), zeros at \(x = \pm 3\).

solution.label: e
steps: The outer branches (\(|x| > 3\)) give two solutions for every \(k > 0\).

Between \(x = -3\) and \(x = 3\), the graph rises from 0 to 4 at \(x = \pm 1\) and dips to 3 at \(x = 0\). A line \(y = k\) with \(3 < k < 4\) meets this part four times; with \(0 < k < 3\) twice; \(k = 3\) three times; \(k = 4\) twice.
Six solutions in all only when \(3 < k < 4\).

stem: This question is about the graphs of \(y = \left|x^2 - 4\right|\) and \(y = 3|x|\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sketch both graphs on the same axes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve the equation \(\left|x^2 - 4\right| = 3x\) for \(x \ge 0\). Hence write down all the solutions of \(\left|x^2 - 4\right| = 3|x|\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Solve the inequality \(\left|x^2 - 4\right| < 3|x|\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Solve the inequality \(\left|x^2 - 4\right| \ge 3|x| + 4\).

idea: Both sides are even functions, so solve for \(x \ge 0\) and reflect. On \(x \ge 0\), \(\left|x^2 - 4\right|\) is \(4 - x^2\) for \(x \le 2\) and \(x^2 - 4\) for \(x \ge 2\): solve each case and keep only the answers in its own interval.

solution.label: a
steps: \(y = \left|x^2 - 4\right|\): zeros at \(\pm 2\), arch up to 4 at \(x = 0\), steep outside. \(y = 3|x|\): a V through the origin with gradients \(\pm 3\).

solution.label: b
steps: Both sides are even, so the solutions of the second equation are \(\pm 1\) and \(\pm 4\).

solution.label: c
steps: For \(x \ge 0\), the V is above the curve between \(x = 1\) and \(x = 4\) (check \(x = 2\): \(0 < 6\)). Reflect for \(x < 0\).
